title: How Long Does a Root Canal Take?
metaTitle: How Long Does a Root Canal Appointment Take?

bodyHtml:
A root canal appointment usually takes somewhere between about 30 and 90 minutes, and more complex cases can run longer or be split across two visits. A front tooth with a single canal is often at the shorter end, while a molar with several canals typically takes more time. The honest answer is that it depends on the tooth, its anatomy, and how much infection is present, so your dentist will give you a time estimate based on your specific situation rather than a one-size-fits-all number.

What affects how long it takes

Several factors influence the length of the appointment:

Which tooth it is. Front teeth and canines usually have one canal, so they tend to be quicker. Premolars often have one or two canals. Molars, the large teeth at the back, can have three or four canals, and cleaning and shaping each one adds time.

Canal anatomy. Some canals are curved, narrow, or unusually shaped, which makes them more time-consuming to clean thoroughly. X-rays help the dentist anticipate this, but every tooth is a little different.

Infection and symptoms. A tooth with significant infection may need extra cleaning, or the dentist may place medication inside and finish at a second visit. This can lengthen the overall process even though each individual appointment is manageable.

Retreatment. Redoing a previous root canal usually takes longer than a first-time treatment because the old filling material must be removed before the canals can be cleaned again.

Your own comfort and pace matter too. If a tooth is tender or hard to numb, a dentist may take extra time to ensure you are comfortable before and during the work, and that care is time well spent.

Why molars take longer than front teeth

The difference mostly comes down to the number and complexity of canals. Treating a single straight canal in a front tooth is relatively direct. A molar, by contrast, may have several canals branching through its roots, each needing to be located, cleaned, shaped, and sealed. More canals simply mean more careful work, which is why a molar root canal often takes noticeably more chair time.

One visit or two?

Many root canals are completed in a single appointment, but some are done over two. A dentist might choose two visits when there is substantial infection, when a tooth is difficult to numb or access, or when it is better to let medication work inside the tooth before sealing it. Neither approach is automatically better; the choice depends on the tooth. If your treatment is split, a temporary filling protects the tooth between visits.

Does a longer appointment mean something is wrong?

Not at all. A longer appointment usually just reflects a tooth with more canals or more complex anatomy. Taking the time to clean each canal properly is part of doing the job well, and a careful, unrushed treatment is what helps the tooth do well afterward.

Will I be uncomfortable lying still that long?

Your dentist can offer breaks, and the tooth is numb throughout. If you find keeping your mouth open tiring, bite blocks can support your jaw. Let your dental team know if you need a pause; the appointment is meant to be as comfortable as possible.

How soon can I get back to my day?

With local anesthetic only, most people return to normal activities the same day, though the area will stay numb for a few hours. If sedation is used, you may need more recovery time and a ride home. Mild soreness for a few days afterward is common and usually settles.
